title: The call in the ear
hook: a newborn's first sounds in this world, and a custom that makes them the call to prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the inward path closed, and your line: polish the heart. Did the trait you named get one small wipe of the cloth? Today a new block begins: the life cycle, from the first day to the last. Day one thousand three hundred eighteen.
screen: `POLISH THE HEART.` · `A NEW BLOCK: THE LIFE CYCLE.`

segments.voice: A hospital room, minutes after a birth. Monitors beeping. Someone crying, someone laughing, someone already on the phone. And in some Muslim families, a father or grandfather leans down close to the baby's right ear and, very softly, says: Allahu akbar. Allah is greater. Then the rest of the call to prayer, whispered, to someone who has never heard a word. The first words, before the name, before anything else. Today: the call in the ear, and where it comes from.
screen: `MINUTES AFTER A BIRTH.` → `A WHISPER IN THE RIGHT EAR.` → `ALLAHU AKBAR, FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the source. It isn't a verse of the Qur'an. It's a report from Abu Rafi', who served the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In Sunan Abu Dawud and Jami' at-Tirmidhi, he says, in paraphrase: I saw the Messenger of Allah give the call to prayer in the ear of al-Hasan ibn 'Ali when Fatimah gave birth to him. Al-Hasan was the Prophet's grandson. So the custom traces back to a grandfather leaning over a newborn. Second, the strength of the report. Tirmidhi graded it sound, and he noted that people acted on it. Some scholars have questioned its chain. So you'll find families who keep the custom carefully and others who don't, and both have reasons. Some families also say the iqamah, the second call that begins a prayer, in the left ear, following other reports. Third, the words themselves. The adhan is the call heard from minarets: Allahu akbar; I bear witness there is no god but Allah; I bear witness Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; come to prayer; come to success. Said to a baby, it's not a summons to get up and pray. It's more like a welcome: the first thing this person hears in the world is the name of Allah and the shape of the life ahead. Fourth, a reflection some readers share. They note that the funeral prayer has no call before it, and say a life is lived between the two: the call whispered at birth, and the prayer said at the end. The time in between is how long it takes to answer.
screen: `ABU RAFI': AL-HASAN'S EAR.` · `A REPORT, GRADED AND DEBATED.` · `THE WORDS OF THE ADHAN.` · `A LIFE BETWEEN CALL AND PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The practice: welcome a new baby, in person or in prayer. Settle, and breathe. Think of a baby born recently, in your family, among friends, or one you only heard about. If no one comes to mind, think of all the babies being born somewhere right now, during this breath. Picture a small face, and the first sounds reaching that ear. If you pray, you can make du'a for that child by name, or simply for every child born today. If not, hold one wish for them: that the first words they hear be kind ones. The bell holds the time.
The call in the ear. The adhan whispered into a newborn's right ear, from the report of Abu Rafi' about al-Hasan, so the first words a child hears are Allahu akbar. Today's word.
screen: `THE CALL IN THE EAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the first words. Today, notice the first words you say to each person you meet, and let at least one of them be a welcome. Tomorrow, the date. Day one thousand three hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: In some Muslim families a parent or elder softly recites the adhan in a newborn's right ear soon after birth, and some also recite the iqamah in the left ear; others do not keep the custom.

what it means: the adhan itself, the call to prayer, softly spoken into the right ear, so Allahu akbar comes first.
